claims.text: Rapidly quenched FeCoNiTi has an fcc matrix containing hexagonal C14 Laves-phase precipitates.
The C14 phase is Ti-rich while the fcc phase is Fe/Co/Ni-rich.
Ti-rich C14 and Fe/Co/Ni-rich fcc sublattices couple antiferromagnetically across their interfaces.
The C14 phase possesses a magnetic moment that is antiparallel to the ferromagnetic fcc phase.
Antiferromagnetic coupling to the C14 phase reduces the net saturation magnetization of the fcc matrix.
Ti 3d states in C14 electronically hybridize with Fe/Co 3d states in the fcc phase.
Proximity to the C14 phase suppresses the orbital and spin moments of the fcc phase.
Rigid C14 precipitates pin magnetic domain walls at fcc/C14 interfaces.
Crystal-structure and thermal-expansion mismatch between C14 and the matrix produces interfacial strain.
Interfacial strain enhances local magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
Domain-wall pinning and induced anisotropy raise coercivity substantially above the single-phase fcc value.
The dual-phase alloy will exhibit approximately 667 Oe coercivity at 400 K.
Single-phase fcc FeCoNi has coercivity capped at 100 Oe because of insufficient orbital moments and the absence of pinning sites.
Effective coercivity enhancement requires a continuous or semi-continuous C14 network that provides sufficient interfacial pinning.
The proposed mechanism can fail when C14 is isolated or when thermal fluctuations overcome the antiferromagnetic coupling.
Spin-polarized DFT will be used to compare the spin density of states at the Fermi level in dual-phase and single-phase samples.
Element-resolved XMCD at the Fe, Co, Ni, and Ti L-edges will be used to determine orbital and spin moments.
A single-phase fcc control with coercivity above 667 Oe at 400 K, no moment reduction in the dual-phase sample, or parallel C14/fcc alignment would falsify the proposed mechanism.
